title: Trust the certificate, not the padlock
summary: Review an expired certificate and a disabled verification path, then explain chain, hostname, and transport rules.

scenario.briefing: The status page started showing certificate warnings. The last deploy added curl -k to the health probe, redirected HTTP to HTTPS but skipped HSTS, and replaced the certificate with one issued for the wrong hostname. Review the change before it spreads to the API.

objectives.description: Identify expired, mismatched, and unverified TLS configuration.
Choose the check a client performs against a certificate.
Explain trust chains, hostnames, and HSTS.

hints: A padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.
The client checks the chain, the dates, and the hostname.
curl -k disables the check you are trying to test.
Fix the certificate and hostname, remove -k, and add HSTS after HTTPS works.

misconceptions.description: Treating the padlock as proof the site is trustworthy.
misconceptions.feedback: A padlock only says the connection is encrypted. It does not prove the operator is honest or the certificate matches the hostname.

misconceptions.description: Believing any valid certificate works for any hostname.
misconceptions.feedback: The client checks that the certificate's subject alternative names cover the hostname it requested. A valid certificate for another host still fails.

misconceptions.description: Adding HSTS before the HTTPS path is correct.
misconceptions.feedback: HSTS tells browsers to refuse HTTP for a period. Enable it only after every subdomain and redirect works over HTTPS, or you lock users out.

sections.title: What the client verifies
sections.body: The client builds a chain to a trusted root, checks the validity dates, and checks that the certificate names the host it requested. A certificate can be valid and still be wrong for this site.

sections.title: Do not disable the check
sections.body: curl -k skips certificate verification. A health probe that uses it will report success while users see a warning. Test the path users take, with verification enabled.

sections.title: HSTS is a commitment
sections.body: HTTP Strict Transport Security tells browsers to use HTTPS for a period, including subdomains if configured. Turn it on after HTTPS and redirects are correct, and start with a short max-age while testing.

findings.label: The health probe disables certificate verification.
The certificate was issued for api.campus.test, not the status hostname.
The HTTPS redirect exists but HSTS is not set.
A padlock in the browser proves the operator is trustworthy.

verdicts.label: Block until the certificate, probe, and HSTS policy are correct

steps.explanation: Renewal alone leaves the hostname mismatch, the verification-disabled probe, and the missing HSTS policy.

steps.title: What does the client check?
steps.prompt: A certificate is unexpired and chains to a trusted root. What else must match?
hints: The certificate lists names it is valid for.
The browser sends the hostname during the handshake.
A valid certificate for another site is still wrong.
The certificate must cover the requested hostname.

quiz.prompt: Which check decides whether this certificate is valid for status.campus.test?

options.label: The certificate's subject alternative names cover status.campus.test
Any unexpired certificate from a trusted root is accepted
The server IP address appears in the certificate

quiz.explanation: Chain and dates are necessary but not sufficient. The certificate must name the host the client requested.

steps.title: Keep transport trust honest
hints: A verification-disabled probe cannot detect the user's failure.
HSTS is enforced by the browser after it sees the header.
Select chain, hostname, verified probes, and HSTS after HTTPS; reject padlock trust and -k.

statements.label: A client checks the certificate chain and validity dates before trusting a connection.
The certificate must cover the hostname the client requested.
Health probes should verify certificates the same way users do.
HSTS should be enabled after HTTPS and redirects are correct.
curl -k is acceptable in production because the connection is still encrypted.
HSTS can safely be enabled before the HTTPS path works.

steps.explanation: Trust depends on chain, dates, hostname, and verified probes. HSTS reinforces HTTPS only after the HTTPS path is correct.

accessibility.summary: Every control is reachable by keyboard, and the checks report text results rather than color alone.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Use Tab to move between controls. Space selects a choice, and Ctrl+Enter runs or submits the active check.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each option, finding, and test announces its label, state, and whether the check passed.
